title: AWS Infrastructure Locations
primary_service: AWS account, infrastructure and billing setup
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of aws infrastructure locations and its relationship to AWS Global Infrastructure and Account Setup.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to aws infrastructure locations.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn aws infrastructure locations in the context of AWS Global Infrastructure and Account Setup. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: AWS Infrastructure Locations matters because it is one part of aws account, infrastructure and billing setup. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: AWS global infrastructure
content_blocks.alt_text: A simplified hierarchy relates Regions, Availability Zones, and workloads while highlighting account and data-residency decisions.
content_blocks.caption: A Region is a geographic area; Availability Zones are separate fault-isolation locations within it.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** AWS Infrastructure Locations belongs to AWS Global Infrastructure and Account Setup. AWS resource placement, account boundaries, access safety, billing visibility and cleanup are one joined workflow. Start with a controlled, approved learning environment.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Edge locations; AWS Local Zones; AWS Wavelength; AWS Outposts and hybrid infrastructure. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For aws infrastructure locations, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Edge locations
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: AWS Local Zones
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: AWS Wavelength
items.text: Write a verification step and a failure case. For hands-on work, start with read-only inspection and use an approved sandbox before changing cloud resources.

items.title: AWS Outposts and hybrid infrastructure
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect available Regions: AWS Infrastructure Locations
content_blocks.code:
# Read-only example related to: AWS Infrastructure Locations
aws ec2 describe-regions --all-regions --query "Regions[].RegionName" --output table
content_blocks.expected_output: A table of Region identifiers available to the caller; service availability still varies by Region.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. For the read-only CLI command, first configure the named profile through an approved credential provider, verify identity, replace example identifiers when required and inspect current official CLI documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “AWS Infrastructure Locations”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for AWS Infrastructure Locations with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: AWS Infrastructure Locations is taught as part of AWS Global Infrastructure and Account Setup.
AWS resource placement, account boundaries, access safety, billing visibility and cleanup are one joined workflow. Start with a controlled, approved learning environment.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
